\section[medius diēs, media nox]{medius diēs, media nox — the source phrase, worn down at different rates}

\label{lesson:LA-C12-medius-dies-nox}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Here's the same Latin phrase, followed into three languages — and each one treated it completely differently.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: The two phrases}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{medius diēs} — literally "\textbf{the middle day}," meaning "\textbf{midday, noon}" (\emph{medius}, "middle" + \emph{diēs}, "day").
  \item \textbf{media nox} — literally "\textbf{the middle night}," meaning "\textbf{midnight}" (\emph{media}, the feminine of \emph{medius} + \emph{nox, noctis}, "night").
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Spanish} kept \textbf{both halves of both phrases} as fully ordinary, living words: \emph{medio/media} ("middle") and \emph{día/noche} ("day/night") — giving \emph{mediodía} and \emph{medianoche}, entirely transparent.
  \item \textbf{French} eroded the \textbf{same phrase unevenly}. \emph{Nox} survived as the everyday word \emph{nuit} ("night") — still fully transparent inside \emph{minuit}. But \emph{diēs} did \textbf{not} survive as French's everyday word for "day" (that's \emph{jour} instead) — so inside \emph{midi}, the \emph{-di} fragment is a fossil, recognizable only from weekday names like \emph{lundi, mardi}, not from any living, standalone word for "day."
  \item \textbf{English} didn't inherit this phrase for "noon" \textbf{at all}. Instead, English's \emph{noon} comes from an entirely different Latin phrase: \textbf{nōna hōra}, "the \textbf{ninth hour}" — originally meaning roughly 3 p.m. (counting from a sunrise start), it drifted steadily earlier over the centuries until it settled on \textbf{midday}.
\end{itemize}

One Latin phrase, three completely different fates: fully kept, half-worn, and simply replaced by another Latin phrase altogether.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "medius diēs" — mid-day, then "media nox" — mid-night{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the three fates — "Spanish kept both halves, French kept only night, English used a different phrase entirely"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "nōna hōra" — the ninth hour — English's real ancestor for "noon"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What do \textbf{medius diēs} and \textbf{media nox} literally mean? ("The middle day" = noon; "the middle night" = midnight.) Which language kept both halves of both phrases fully transparent? (\textbf{Spanish} — \emph{mediodía, medianoche}.) Which language kept "night" but not "day"? (\textbf{French} — \emph{nuit} stayed alive, \emph{-di} became a fossil.) Does English's \emph{noon} come from this same phrase? (\textbf{No} — from \emph{nōna hōra}, "the ninth hour," which drifted from afternoon to midday.)
\end{tcolorbox}
